text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Culturally safe, trauma-informed care: ask how he wishes to be addressed and what matters to him, offer the Lakota interpreter, take time, explain each examination and ask consent first, and do not probe his history or beliefs beyond what he chooses to share
  • Orthopaedic foot and ankle consultation at the clinic's visiting specialist session to confirm the diagnosis and explain every treatment option, including surgery
  • Imaging: weight-bearing X-rays today; CT if they show arthritis or metal, to map the joints and any fragments; blood lead only if fragments are found, since fragments in a joint or bone raise lead levels
  • Pain: diclofenac gel first; an oral NSAID for a limited time only after home blood pressure and kidney function are checked; acetaminophen if needed; no opioids, which the Indian Health Service advises against as an initial treatment for chronic pain
  • A rigid ankle-foot orthosis that holds the hindfoot, a rocker-sole shoe for the other days, a cane in the right hand, and six weeks of physical therapy with a home exercise program
  • Ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection of the subtalar joint if pain stays above 4 of 10 after four to six weeks; no more than three or four a year
  • Surgery (subtalar or double arthrodesis) explained with shared decision-making: what it can and cannot do, months of recovery and the effect on riding; the choice is his, and it is offered again if pain stops him walking or riding
  • Prediabetes: walking and riding as the foot allows, fewer refined foods and more vegetables and traditional foods, the clinic's diabetes prevention program funded by the Special Diabetes Program for Indians, and hemoglobin A1c again in three to four months
  • Blood pressure: home readings twice daily for a week with a clinic monitor before the next visit, since one raised clinic reading does not make a diagnosis
  • Emotional well-being: depression screening with the PHQ-2 and PHQ-9; grief and anger about real losses are not treated as a disorder; behavioral health and traditional healing are available whenever he chooses, side by side with clinic care
  • Food: the Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations (which offers bison and other traditional foods) or SNAP, garden support, and the Community Health Representative to help with forms
  • Getting to care: rides from the Community Health Representative program and physical therapy by video on the weeks he cannot travel

resource.title: Sitting Bull synthetic care plan
resource.description: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the hindfoot decades after a gunshot wound, in a 55-year-old Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man seen at a clinic serving the Standing Rock Reservation. The episode covers culturally safe, trauma-informed care that asks his preferences, offers a Lakota interpreter and traditional healing alongside Western care without probing his beliefs, as the Indian Health Service policy asks; weight-bearing X-rays and CT; retained bullet fragments, when they raise blood lead and why these do not; pain treatment led by a topical NSAID, a short oral NSAID course and no opioids; a rigid ankle-foot orthosis, physical therapy and an ultrasound-guided subtalar injection under the ACR/Arthritis Foundation guideline and the CMID osteoarthritis monograph; surgical options (arthrodesis) explained with shared decision-making and his decision to wait respected; an NSAID-related dyspepsia; screening for diabetes, high blood pressure and depression in a man who has lived through forced displacement, exile, hunger and imprisonment, without turning grief for real losses into a diagnosis; prediabetes; and food insecurity on a commodity diet, with the Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations, traditional foods and the Community Health Representative program.
